scenes.script_line: Look at the ground beneath your boots. Just dirt? Look closer. There are roots, fungi and tiny living organisms, working even when we cannot see them. A building starts with foundations. Nature has foundations too. Before you move the earth, remember: you are working on a living system, not an empty surface.

macro of roots and small insects in turned earth
crew member crouching to look closely at the ground before digging
wide shot of a garden plot with foreman pointing at the earth

scenes.script_line: A mature tree gives shade on a hot working day. Its roots help hold the soil. Its branches shelter birds. And its fallen leaves feed the life beneath it. How long would it take us to replace everything that tree does? Before parking a machine near it, pause. Some things are worth protecting precisely because we cannot rebuild them tomorrow.

shots.text: wide shot of a mature tree shading two crew members on a hot day
close-up of tree roots holding soil in place
medium shot of a worker carefully steering a wheelbarrow around a tree
close-up of fallen leaves gathered at the base of a tree

scenes.script_line: A leaf falls. Small organisms help break it down. The soil gains organic matter. Roots grow, and another leaf appears. Nature is full of connections. Construction is too: a small mistake in one task can affect the next team. When we understand connections, we make better decisions. Look beyond today's job. Ask what your actions affect next.

foreman guiding one apprentice pointing down the garden row

must_not: isolated worker with no connection to others

scenes.script_line: Two teams build the same wall beside a tree. One puts materials wherever there is space. The other checks the ground and protects the root area first. Both might finish the wall. But which team has finished responsibly? Quality is not only the straightness of a wall. It is also the care taken for everything around it.

scenes.script_line: Tomorrow, before starting the machine, spend ten seconds looking around. Where does water flow? Is there a young plant? Is loose packaging blowing away? Ten seconds will not complete the work. But they may help prevent a problem that takes hours to correct. Awareness begins with attention. Notice first. Then act.
